query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under elevated-temperature exposure, the reactive gas environment (oxidizing versus reducing) promotes the diffusion and segregation of reactive alloying elements (especially Al and Ti) to grain boundaries where they form brittle oxide or intermetallic precipitates. These localized changes weaken grain boundary cohesion and serve as crack initiation sites, ultimately causing catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a uniform FCC matrix and typical AM-induced microstructural heterogeneities.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the gas atmosphere during high-temperature exposure by replacing an oxidizing environment with a reducing (or inert) one, while keeping the temperature and exposure time constant.
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (approximately 700–982 °C) under controlled oxidizing and reducing atmospheres for durations long enough to allow noticeable diffusion and precipitation phenomena.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries where segregation of Al and Ti leads to the formation of brittle precipitates (e.g., oxides or intermetallic phases).
generation.mechanism: The reactive gas atmosphere enhances element mobility by facilitating oxidation (or a lack thereof in reducing conditions), which drives Al and Ti to segregate and form brittle phases at the grain boundaries. Under oxidizing conditions, the formation of refractory oxides is more pronounced, compromising grain boundary integrity. This embrittlement leads to stress concentration and rapid crack propagation once critical damage accumulates, explaining the observed catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline state, specimens exposed in an oxidizing atmosphere will exhibit increased grain boundary precipitate formation, lower ductility, and earlier onset of catastrophic failure. In contrast, specimens exposed in a reducing (or inert) atmosphere should show less segregation/precipitation and retain higher toughness under the same thermal conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured alloy before extended high-temperature exposure, characterized by minimal grain boundary segregation or precipitate formation and retention of designed ductility.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for exposures at temperatures within the 700–982 °C range and atmospheres with controlled oxygen partial pressures versus reducing gas compositions. Results outside these parameters may involve additional degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of element diffusion, precipitate composition, and the quantitative difference in mechanical property degradation between oxidizing and reducing conditions are not precisely known and require experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical specimens of the AM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy and expose them to a constant high-temperature profile within the 700–982 °C range under three different gas atmospheres: (1) oxidizing, (2) reducing, and (3) inert. After exposure for a fixed duration, conduct microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM and EDS mapping) to quantify grain boundary segregation and precipitate formation. Perform mechanical tests (tensile and fracture toughness) to compare ductility and failure behavior across conditions.
measurements: Grain boundary chemistry and precipitate identification (EDS, XRD, TEM)
Mechanical properties: tensile ductility, fracture toughness, and time-to-failure under load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant differences in grain boundary segregation, precipitate formation, and subsequent mechanical degradation (ductility reduction and earlier catastrophic failure) are observed between the oxidizing and reducing (or inert) conditions compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract The corrosion behavior of the FCC Cr 18 Mn 27 Fe 27.5 Ni 27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours, has been investigated. Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt. The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation. Thermal exposure at 700 °C for 1000 hours also led to the precipitation of an additional BCC phase Cr 67 Fe 13 Mn 18.5 Ni 1.5 , which was confirmed by CALPHAD predictions. Subject terms: Structural materials, Metals and alloys
